They were translated into English by the same Venerable monk, presently residing at Potkulkala Forest Hermitage in Khandagedra Devalagam.

With the permission of the Most Venerable Great Preceptor and the Assembly of the Venerable Mediterranean monks, this is the 24th sermon in the series of sermons on Nibbana.

In our last sermon we brought up a quotation from the Rohita Sutra which enshrines a momentous declaration by the Buddha to the effect that the world, the arising of the world, the cessation of the world and the path leading to the cessation of the world could be pointed out with reference to this same body with its perceptions and mind.

The six sense fears or the six basis of sense contact with which we acquaint ourselves with the world as it is conventionally understood and measured out are themselves called the world according to the noble one's terminology.
Therefore, one can declare in accordance with the Dhamma that the very cessation of those six sense fears is the cessation of the world.
It is this state of the cessation of the world that is known as Asankhata Dhatu or the Unprepared Element.
That Unprepared State described in this course on Nibbana in such terms as Atibikali Adyatanga Bhutanga Katanga Samkhata,
Man's Dhyas and Unborn and Unbecome and Unmade and Unprepared is the cessation of the six spheres of sense which is the end of that prepared world.
So then, this particular world's sense, the end of the world as defined here, is not a destination to be reached by travelling.
The sage Rohitasa walked for hundred years in search of this world's sense at the speed of a flying arrow but he failed to discover the world's sense.
Why? It is because he took the world along with him in his journey to see its sense.
Since this six base body with its perceptions and mind is itself the world, he was taking the world with him in his exploration.
That is why he had to die on the way without seeing the end of the world.
That end of the world which one cannot see or reach by travelling, the Buddha pointed out in the very cessation of the six sense fears.
This fact comes to light in the discourses leading with Nibbāna in the Pataligami Avaga of the Udhan, which we had already discussed.

I say there is neither coming, nor going, nor standing, nor passing away, nor being reborn.
That state which is unestablished, non-continuing and objectless is itself the end of suffering.
So then, this journey is end, the journey is end that cannot be reached by journey, the Buddha pointed out in the cessation of the six sense fears.

Wavering not being, there is calm. Calm being, there is no inclination. Inclination not being, there is no coming and going. Coming and going not being, there is no passing away or reappearing. When there is no passing away or reappearing, there is neither here nor there, nor anything between the two.

This is the end of Sahra. It is in such profound terms that the Buddha described the end of the world. One cannot see it by journeying. It can be seen only by wisdom. In fact, even the very concept of going has to be transcended in order to see it.

So, it seems, Rohitasa carried the world with him in his journey to see the end of the world. He made another brand. He was going in search of a place where there is no death, in order to escape death.
Even that, the Buddha had declared, is not possible to see or reach by travelling. Rohitasa took Mara along with him in his journey to find a place where there is no death. Why do we say so?
In the Raja Samyutta of the Samyutta Nikaya, we find Venerable Radha, putting the following question to the Buddha.
Maro Maroti Bhante Vujyati Kitavatanukho Bhante Maroti Vujyati
Mar Mara Mara, they say, Venerable say. To what extent is Mara called as such?
Now, this is how the Buddha answers the question.
When there is form Radha, there would be Mara.
Mara, O one who kills, O one who dies.
Therefore, rather, in this context, you look upon form as Mara, as one who kills, as one who dies, as a disease, as a vile, as a doubt, as a misery, as a wretchedness.
They that look upon thus, are those that see rightly.
As in the case of form, so also, in regard to feeling, perception, preparations and consciousness, the same mode of seeing rightly is recommended.
So, in this context, each of the five aggregates is looked upon as a Mara from the point of view of the Dharma.
That is why we say that Rohitasa went in search of a deathless place, taking death alone with him.
From this definition, it is clear that so long as one grasps with craving the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, preparations and consciousness, there is a Mara, a killer and one who dies.
Therefore, it is, that by giving up the five aggregates, one is free from Mara, is liberated from death and attains the deathless state.
That is why we say that the Arahanta has attained the deathless state here and now in this world itself.

The tendency to grasp a sign in regard to the objects of the six senses is the result of the perception of permanence.
Due to the perception of permanence, there is a grasping of signs.
And due to that grasping of signs, influxes flow in.
Proliferations through craving, conceits and views get heaped up.
This is how our world is constructed.
This is the way the aggregates of attachment get accumulated.
On the other hand, the contemplation of impermanence that leads to the signless concentration is helpful in freeing the mind from these signs.
The reflection on an object can be of two types.
Where there is a perception of permanence, the tendency is to grasp the object tenaciously and hang on to it.
This pervert tendency is known as Paramasana.
It is impelled by the triple proliferation of craving, conceits and fears.
Under its influence, one is carried away by prolific perceptions, Papancha Sanya,
Sankha, and is kept under the sway of worldly concepts and designations born of prolific perceptions, Papancha Sanya, Sankha.
On the contrary, the perception of impermanence fosters a detached and observant attitude in reflection, which is known as Sammasana.
It is that healthy attitude which progressively leads to the liberation of the mind from the influence of signs and attenuates the prolific tendencies to craving, conceits and fears.
This kind of reflection is the harbinger of insight.
Contemplation is the harbinger of insight.

The perception of impermanence on these lines effectively puts an end to this entire mass of samsaric suffering, as is evident from the following powerful declaration by the Buddhas in the Khanda-sangat.

The contemplation of impermanence, therefore, strikes at the very root of this entire mass of samsaric suffering.

Thus Marx, the Tathagata doing such, in regard to all phenomena, seen, heard, sensed and cognized, is such. Moreover than he who is such, there is none other higher or more excellent, I declare.
What have I seen, heard, sensed, or crowned to an esteemed as truth by other folk? Meant those who are entrenched in their own lives, being such, I hold none as true or false.
This barb I build well in advance, whereon mankind is hooked, impaled, I know I see it is fairly so, no such claim for the Tathagata.

In the first statement, the Buddha declares that he knows tamahan jnanami, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, thoughted after and pondered over by all beings in the world, and that is the sum total of the knowledge acquired through the sixth sense basis.
In the second statement, he affirms that the knowledge he has is of a higher order.

The third statement flows from this detached perspective. It is to the effect that the Tathagata cannot disclaim knowledge despite his detached attitude, as it would be tantamount to prevarication in the eyes of the world.
The fourth statement highlights the same incongruity because the Tathagata placed in this awkward situation cannot compromise by both claiming and disclaiming knowledge at the same time.
As the fifth statement makes it clear, the Tathagata does not deem it fit to wriggle out by neither claiming nor disclaiming knowledge of sense data.
Then comes the declaration as to how the Tathagata treats this body of sensory knowledge of the world.
Thus, the Tathagata does not imagine visible things apart from the sea.
We have come across the terms ditta, sutte, mutte, vinyata, vinyata quite often.
For instance, in our discussion of the Baja sutra in the context, itte ditta mattaṁ bhavisati, sutte sutta mattaṁ bhavisati, mutte mutta mattaṁ bhavisati, vinyata vinyata mattaṁ bhavisati.
In the scene there will be just the scene, in the heard there will be just the third, in the sense there will be just the sense, in the cognized there will be just the cognized.
In common parlance, the word seen connotes something seen, but here we have something more radical, avoiding substantialist insinuations.
It is just the scene in the scenes, implied by ditta, in this context too.
The Tathagata takes it just as a scene, without imagining that there is something substantial, worthwhile scene, as a part from it.
ditta dattaṁ bhavang dittaṁ namanyati.
We are already familiar with the term manjana, having discussed it in such discourses as the Moolaparya sutte and the Baja sutte.
It stands for imaginings, prompted by cravings, conceits and views.
Tathagata is free from such imaginings.
He does not imagine a thing worthwhile seeing, apart from the seeing.
Nor does he imagine an unseen, adittaṁ namanyati.
The phenomenon of seeing is not denied.
The phrase dattaṁ bhavang dittaṁ namanyati conveys the idea that the Tathagata does not imagine that there is something worth seeing.

Yet there is something essential in it. That Tharana-magnati, he does not imagine a seer or one who sees. He does not project an agent into the phenomenon by taking seriously the subject-object relationship.
With regard to the heard, sutta, the sensed, mutha and the cognized vinyata too, the Tharana-magnati has no such imagination. Then in summing up it is said,
Thus marks the Tharana being such in regard to all phenomena, seen, heard, sensed and cognized, is such. The term Tharana too came up in a number of our earlier assignments. We rendered it by such.
It stands for the quality of steadfastness of the Aran in remaining unshaken by the eight worldly vicissitudes. His mainstay in this respect is Atam-meta or non-identification.
He is such because he does not draft any of those things as mine. So he is such in regard to whatever is seen, heard, sensed and cognized.
There is no one who is higher or more excellent than the such-like one in point of certainness. Then comes a couplet of verses presenting the gist of the sermon.
Our rendering of the sermon is in need of further explication. Though it gives a general idea, some words and phrases in the original have far-reaching implications.
The basic idea behind the series of declarations made is the extraordinary change of attitude towards the question of speculative views, which marks off the Tathagata from all his contemporaries.
He took a completely different turn, transcending the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism.
This difference of attitude is revealed by the Ridley's statements in the first part of the discourse.
One gets the impression that the Tathagata was confronted with the problematic situation of the high story.

The first statement is to the effect that the Tathagata knows whatever in the world, with its gods, Maharas and Brahmas, among the prajini consisting of recluses and Brahmins, gods and men, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, thought after and pondered over by the mind.
The second statement asserts that the Tathagata has a higher understanding of all that. All the same, he takes no stance in regard to whatever is seen, heard, sensed and cognized.
This might appear as a riddle. Usually, when one has a higher understanding of something, one is inclined to take one's stand upon it.
But here we have a denial. The discourse bears some resemblance to the tetralema we had discussed earlier.
But there seems to be a difference here in the formulation of the first proposition of the tetralema.
Normally, the first proposition amounts to an unqualified assertion of the affirmative standpoint.
In this case, however, we find the statement that the Tathagata not only knows all what the world knows, but that he has a higher understanding of it.
It is precisely because he has a higher understanding that he takes no stance in regard to it.
This might appear problematic. But let us remind ourselves of the two levels of understanding mentioned in the Mura Pariyasutra discussed earlier, namely Sanjanati and Abhijanati.
As an instance of the first level of understanding, we get the following passage in the discourse in regard to the untaught ordinary person.
As an instance of the Tathagata and Abhijanati and Abhijanati and Abhijanati and Abhijanati.
If earth is mine, he delights in earth.
The untaught ordinary person has a perceptual knowledge of earth, Sanjana.
That too is a level of knowledge.
It is in fact the lowest grade of knowing.
The untaught ordinary person can do no better than perceive earth as earth.
Having perceived earth as earth, he takes it seriously by its face value
and goes on imagining by way of craving, conceit and views, granting it object status.
He imposes the grammatical superstructure on it.
He imagines on the earth, he imagines from the earth, he imagines earth is mine, he delights in earth.
This then is the lowest grade of knowledge.
On the other hand, about the Tathagata's level of understanding, the Moolapariya Supta has the following description.
Patareng patavito abhijanati, patareng patavito abhijanati, patareng namanyati, patareng namanyati, patareng nabhinandati.
He understands through higher knowledge earth as earth.
Having understood through higher knowledge earth as earth, he does not imagine earth to be earth.
He does not imagine on the earth, he does not imagine from the earth, he does not imagine earth is mine, he does not delight in earth.
The Tathagata who has a higher knowledge of earth, as suggested by the word abhijanati, does not entertain imaginings by taking earth at its face value.
He is not carried away by the grammatical structure to imagine in such terms as on the earth and from the earth.
In the present context too, the same distinction in grades of knowledge is evident.
Firstly, the Tathagata says, all that do I know, that have I fully understood, all that is known to the Tathagata.
It is precisely because of this full understanding that he has not taken his stand upon.
He has no stance in regard to all that.
This is the gist of the first paragraph of the discourse, which sounds more or less a paradox.
It is because of this apparently clear state of awareness that the Tathagata had to confess that it would be a falsehood on his part to say all that I do not know.
If someone asks whether it is because he does not know that he takes no stance, he cannot say yes.
As a matter of fact, it is precisely because he has understood that he takes no stance.
But the warnings are of the opinion that knowledge of a thing entitles one to assert it dogmatically.
To say, I both know it and know it not, I neither know it nor am ignorant of it, could also be mistaken by the word as a prevarication or equivocation.
The first paragraph of the discourse has to be understood in this slide.
The commentary has it that the earth should at five points in the discourse.

According to it, the three significant terms, Janami, Abhanyasi and Biritam, I know, I have fully understood, all that is known to the Tathagata, represent a plane of omniscience, sabbanyutabhuri, peculiar to Buddha.
Even at the end of this proclamation of omniscience, it is said the earth should as a mark of approbation.
Then the phrase, Naupaktasi, does not take his stand upon it, is interpreted by the commentary as indicating the plane of the influx-free one, Kinasabhuri.
Why the Tathagata has no stance in regard to sensory data is said to be due to his freedom from influxes.
He does not cast them by way of craving, conceit and views.
He does not take his stand upon things seen, heard, sensed and organised.
He has no intention of clinging towards them.
